title: Heuristic Reflective Chain-of-Thought: Enhancing Multi-Step Reasoning in Large Language Models With  Reflection and Heuristic Guidance

items.publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
items.abstract: Arabic Large Language Models exhibit a pronounced deficit in multi-stepreasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and agentic planning relative to their En-glish counterparts - a gap we attribute to the scarcity of high-quality Arabic chain-of-thought (CoT) training data and suboptimal tokenization of Arabic script. Wepresent AraCoT-Agent, a rigorous framework for distilling structured reasoning ca-pabilities from frontier teacher models (DeepSeek-R1, QwQ-32B) into smaller, de-ployable Arabic-focused models via reward-weighted supervised fine-tuning. Cen-tral to our approach is AraCoT, the first curated, quality-filtered Arabic reason-ing trace dataset constructed through a five-stage filtering pipeline that enforces an-swer correctness (ε ≤ 10−3), fluency bounds via AraBERT perplexity, structuralcompleteness, and near-duplicate removal using MinHash-based Jaccard similarity.We formalize the training objective as a GRPO-style reward-weighted cross-entropyloss with composite reward r(x, c) = λ1 · 1[correct] + λ2 · |c|/Lmax + λ3 · fluency(c),which down-weights gradients for already high-quality examples. We further intro-duce AraAgent-Bench, a 500-problem benchmark spanning five agentic reasoningtask types across five difficulty tiers, with formal difficulty defined by minimum solu-tion steps. Through controlled experiments comparing QLoRA fine-tuning (rank 64,4-bit NF4) on Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B against full fine-tuning on Qwen3-4B,we demonstrate that our best model achieves a 55.7% relative improvement over thestrongest baseline (Llama3-8B base, 30.0%) on AraAgent-Bench ((46.7-30.0)/30.0 ×100; p < 0.05, McNemar’s test), substantially closing the Arabic-English reasoninggap. Ablation studies reveal that data quality dominates quantity, GRPO weightingyields consistent gains over standard SFT, and tokenization efficiency (ρQwen ≈ 1.8vs. ρLlama ≈ 3.2 tokens per Arabic word) is a significant predictor of cross-lingualreasoning transfer.

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in reasoning tasks through the Chain of Thought (CoT) prompting technology, but their large scale makes it difficult to deploy them in resource-constrained environments. This paper explores the transfer of the reasoning capabilities of large models to small models through CoT Distillation to enhance the complex reasoning performance of the small models. The study uses the OpenR1-Math-220k dataset generated by DeepSeek R1 as the "teacher reasoning process" source, and employs the QLoRA parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique to train on the Qwen3-8B small model. Experimental results show that the fine-tuned model achieves an accuracy of 10% on the AIME-level mathematics test set compared to the baseline model, and can generate structured reasoning steps. The study verifies the effectiveness of CoT Distillation and provides a reproducible baseline framework for the deployment of small models in reasoning tasks. The paper hopes to provide researchers with future research directions.</jats:p>
title: Enhancing the Mathematical Reasoning Ability of Small Language Models through Thought Chain Distillation

items.abstract: <jats:p>Chain-of-thought prompting improves answers by generating the reasoning first. We study the inverse: does providing the outcome first improve the reasoning? A naive inversion is impractical-obtaining the full answer can be as hard as the original problem, and given the answer, the reasoning may no longer be needed. We instead condition on a minimal proxy: a single binary tag (Y/N) indicating whether the forthcoming reasoning chain succeeds (equivalently, in our construction, whether the problem is solvable). Training transformer language models from scratch on a controlled combinatorial arithmetic task: five given numbers must be connected in order by binary operators to reach a target, so each problem admits exactly 2⁴ = 16 (operators +,-) or 4⁴ = 256 (operators +,-, ×, ÷) operator permutations, and exhaustive enumeration yields an exact random-guess baseline for every test item. Holding data, architecture, and optimization fixed, we compare placing this tag before versus after the reasoning chain across two task regimes (two operators, 16 permutations, 20k training steps; four operators, 256 permutations, 50k steps). Despite indistinguishable training loss, tag-before models produce significantly more correct reasoning chains in free generation, and the tag acts as a controllable goal signal at inference: forcing Y yields up to 30× the exact chance baseline on single-solution problems (versus 18× for tag-after), while forcing N suppresses correct chains to-and in the easier regime, below-chance. The dissociation between flat next-token loss and rising, formatdependent reasoning accuracy indicates that training loss can be a poor proxy for reasoning capability. One bit of anticipated outcome, placed before generation, reshapes what function the model computes.</jats:p>
title: Inverse Chain-of-Thought: A One-Bit Outcome Tag Before Reasoning Improves the Reasoning Itself
